property_summary: For any caller and any timestamp/block number, when fallback is called with exactly 10 ether the reference contract always accepts (does not revert) and updates pastBlockTime to block.timestamp; the mutant that requires 9 ether will reject calls sending 10 ether, so there exist inputs (amount = 10 ether) where the mutant reverts but the reference does not.

For any caller, when the fallback is invoked with exactly 10 ether the reference C accepts the call (does not revert) and updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp (so the getter pastBlockTime equals block.timestamp after the call), whereas the mutant that requires 9 ether will revert on a 10 ether call and thus fail this property for that input.

For any caller and any amount, when the fallback is invoked with an amount different from 10 ether the reference contract will revert iff the amount != 10 ether, so specifically the reference accepts calls sending exactly 10 ether (updating pastBlockTime) while the mutant that expects 9 ether will revert on 10 ether; the test asserts that calling fallback with any fuzzed amount yields success exactly when amount == 10 ether (a property the reference satisfies for all inputs and the mutant breaks for some inputs).

For every call that sends exactly 9 ether, the buggy mutant accepts (does not revert) but the reference rejects; equivalently, the reference contract always reverts when sent 9 ether to its fallback, while the mutant would accept some of those inputs — so the invariant is: calling fallback with amount == 9 ether always reverts on the correct contract.

For every call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether, the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime only when the current block.timestamp is strictly greater than the previous pastBlockTime; the mutant updates pastBlockTime regardless, so there exist inputs (same timestamp replays) where the mutant's pastBlockTime equals the call timestamp even when it should not change.

For any caller and any timestamp, if a call to fallback succeeds with msg.value == 10 ether, then the reference contract only updates pastBlockTime when block.timestamp is strictly greater than the previous pastBlockTime; the mutant unconditionally updates pastBlockTime, so when two sequential calls occur with the same timestamp the mutant's pastBlockTime will change on the second call while the reference's will not.

For any caller and any timestamp, after any successful payable fallback call with msg.value == 10 ether, the reference contract only updates pastBlockTime if the current block.timestamp is strictly greater than the stored pastBlockTime; the mutant unconditionally updates pastBlockTime, so repeated successful calls at the same timestamp will leave pastBlockTime unchanged in the reference but changed in the mutant.

For any two sequential successful fallback calls that send exactly 10 ether, if the second call occurs at the same block.timestamp as the first, the reference C preserves pastBlockTime (it does not advance on the second call) while the mutant advances pastBlockTime; the test fuzzes caller and a boolean deciding whether to make the second call in the same timestamp to detect the mutant.

For any successful payable fallback call (msg.value == 10 ether), the reference contract only updates pastBlockTime when block.timestamp is strictly greater than the stored pastBlockTime; the mutant unconditionally updates pastBlockTime, so there exist sequences of two calls at the same timestamp where the mutant's pastBlockTime changes on the second call but the reference's does not.

After any successful call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether at a strictly later block.timestamp, the stored pastBlockTime equals the block.timestamp (i.e., pastBlockTime is set to the timestamp by the reference); the mutant that stores block.number instead will sometimes leave pastBlockTime not equal to the timestamp, violating this rule.

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether from any caller at a strictly later timestamp, the reference contract only drains its balance when block.number % 15 == 0 (so address(c).balance == 0 iff block.number % 15 == 0 after the call); the mutant instead drains for block.number % 15 != 0, violating this invariant for some block numbers.

For any caller and any block where block.timestamp increases and msg.value == 10 ether, whenever block.number % 15 == 0 the reference C will transfer the entire contract balance to the caller (leaving address(c).balance == 0), whereas the mutant returns only msg.value and can leave a nonzero contract balance; the test asserts address(c).balance == 0 after such a call.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether at a strictly later timestamp when block.number % 15 == 0, the correct contract forwards the entire contract balance (leaving address(c).balance == 0) after the fallback call; the mutant that transfers only msg.value can leave a positive contract balance, violating this rule.

Whenever fallback is invoked with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime and block.number % 15 == 0, the reference contract empties its own balance (address(c).balance == 0) after the call by transferring the entire contract balance to the caller; the mutant that transfers only msg.value can leave a non-zero contract balance, violating this rule.

For any caller X sending exactly 10 ether to C's fallback at a strictly later timestamp, if block.number % 15 == 0 then the reference contract forwards to X at least the incoming msg.value (so address(c).balance does not increase as a result of that call); the mutant that only transfers msg.value can leave the contract balance increased when prior balance > 0, breaking this property.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether at a strictly later timestamp when block.number % 15 == 0, the reference contract forwards the contract's entire balance (leaving address(c).balance == 0) while the mutant that transfers only msg.value can leave a positive contract balance.
